campaigns.title: Nourish a Child. Nurture Their Future.
campaigns.description: Every child deserves a healthy start in life.Good nutrition and healthcare are essential for a child's growth, learning and development. Yet, for children growing up in migrant and underserved communities, access to both remains a challenge.In Hyderabad's urban settlements and brick kiln communities, families face difficult living and working conditions, with limited access to nutritious food and basic healthcare. This affects children's health, growth and ability to learn.At Youth Feed Foundation, we believe that a child's circumstances should not determine their opportunity to grow, learn and thrive.What Your Contribution SupportsYour donation will support two Youth Feed Foundation programmes:Project Gyan Shakthi: Supporting children attending community learning centres.Project Brick Kiln: Supporting young children and adolescents living in migrant brick kiln communities.Through these programmes, we provide:This Children's Day, Help Us Reach More ChildrenThanks to our matching restaurant partners from NRAI Hyderabad, every contribution will be matched, strengthening the nutrition and healthcare support provided to each child.Every contribution, big or small, helps us reach more children with the nutrition and healthcare they need.Support a child today. Help us reach 1,500 children.#YFFChildrensDay2026Please note: WE ACCEPT ONLY INDIAN DONATIONSAs per Foreign Contribution Regulation Act 2010, we cannot accept donations from Foreign Citizens, OCI/PIO card holders, or Indian citizens residing outside India. Please donate only if you do not fall in these categories.

campaigns.title: Runway of Hope 2026 | Support India's Government Schools
campaigns.description: A child enters the school halls with open eyes, ears, and heart. Learning every day. Learning how to say hi, be friends, and help each other.Learning ABC, 1+1, and what keeps plants alive? (Hint: it’s the sun)Learning how to dream:I want to become the president and give shelter to people who sleep on streetsI want to be a gamer and make my parents proudI will be a teacher and teach children who can’t afford schoolBut here’s what happens. Many fail to gain foundational learning skills; they can’t read or comprehend sentences, or even do simple 2-digit subtraction by age 8. Only 30% of them go on to pursue higher education. These children could have been the next big scientist, researcher, or director of India. But they fall victim to an unequal education system that makes circumstances matter more than their potential. Today, 140 million children in India study in primary Government schools.  There are children in these schools with dreams, but at the risk of losing their shot at a prosperous, thriving future. There is one way we can save millions of futures: teachersOne great teacher can shift a student's academic trajectory.But India’s teachers are crushed under a wide range of responsibilities and little support. Teachers carry the state’s aspirations for a high-quality education system, but do not receive the support and systems that can enable them. In 2025, NCERT (PARAKH) reported that only 35% of teachers in India received any professional development.Teachers are bent over backward trying to do their best and always looking for ways to do more:It was a dream to see my class read a book. For years I wasn't able to do it. Today 60% of them can.My grade 3 children used to feel so underconfident in English; it wasn’t just about ability, but just this hesitation. Today, they can read English paragraphs, and they are more confident and outspokenI used to focus on what children couldn’t do, but never really thought about where I could get better, and what I needed to change. I am starting to reflect and do that nowThat is the work. Teachers learning, re-learning & trying. At SEF, we work with the one person in that classroom who can change what happens next.6 programs across 3 states, building the training, coaching, and classroom resources that teachers were always supposed to have.90% relevance score for our trainings and 2x learning outcomes Today, we work with 2 lakh current and future teachers and 3M children.By 2030, we will work with one million. That's millions more children with a chance of a better future.That is the runway we are building. Every teacher on it is carrying a room full of children who still believe they are going to be president, or a gamer, or the teacher who comes back for the kids who can't pay.By donating, you are not just funding one teacher or one classroom. You are funding every classroom those 2 lakh teachers will ever walk into, and every child who has a dream.The future is in their hands.

campaigns.title: Sponsor a Safety Workbook This Children’s Day
campaigns.description: Safe Schools works with schools and communities across Tamil Nadu and Karnataka. As part of this work, we reach 462 children across two communities in Cuddalore and 45 girls at an orphanage.The children in Cuddalore come from families who work hard to support their education, including those engaged in fishing, domestic work and small industries. The girls at the home are cared for by a devoted team, and some have no family of their own.Every one of these children deserves to know how to stay safe, how to say no and who to turn to. Our workbooks help them learn this through Ira and her friends, with real situations matched to their age and space to draw, write, play and share how they feel.Educators and caregivers in both communities tell us that children enjoy learning with Ira and her friends, and that the workbooks are helping them speak up with confidence.This Children’s Day, you can help us reach more children in these two communities. ₹220 gives one child a workbook. ₹5,500 covers a class of 25 children. Every gift is 80G eligible.Please donate and share this page with someone who cares about children.

campaigns.title: Empower 50 care leavers by supporting their education and livelihood
campaigns.description: The Day He Turned 18On the day Karan (pseudonym) turned 18, the system said he was an adult.But nothing else changed. He still had no family to call when he felt lost.No savings account. No laptop. No one to guide him through college applications. No one to explain how rent works, how interviews work, how life works.For most of us, adulthood comes slowly. For a child growing up in institutional care, it arrives overnight.At 18, support ends. But adulthood has just begun. And that gap is where futures are lost.What Happens After Care?Every year in India, thousands of young people age out of Child Care Institutions. At CLAN, we do not see “beneficiaries.” We see young adults with dreams who simply need the same safety net most of us were born into.We provide:Education sponsorship and fee supportCareer guidance and employability trainingEmotional and mentorship supportEmergency financial assistanceA long-term ecosystem that stays even after 18What Your Donation Actually Does₹3,000 can cover application fees and documentation for higher education.₹10,000 can support one month of safe housing.₹25,000 can keep a student in college for an entire semester.But more than money, your donation says:“You are not alone.”For someone who has grown up without a permanent support system, that sentence changes everything.

campaigns.title: Help abandoned elderly with shelter and care
campaigns.description: 1 in 4 elders in urban India is abused by their own son or daughter-in-law.Every day, elderly parents are left alone on streets, at railway stations, even outside temples. Many are sick, have little money and struggle with age-related illnesses. Often it takes weeks or months before the painful truth comes out: they were abandoned by their own families.Indian law makes it mandatory for children and relatives to care for senior citizens. Yet elder abuse and abandonment continue to rise.Why are elders being abandoned?Changing families: The joint family once had room for elders, cared for across generations. With rapid urbanisation and nuclear families, many elders are now isolated, neglected or abandoned.Poverty and poor healthcare: Small pensions and limited healthcare leave elders dependent on their families. As their health declines and costs rise, many face abuse and abandonment, especially women and widows.How our NGO partners help Our NGO partners work on the ground to rescue abandoned elders and give them shelter, care and dignity. Through old age homes across India, these seniors get to live their golden years in peace, comfort and security, surrounded by compassion.Your donation will help:Fund rescue operations to bring more elders off the streetsProvide shelter, food, healthcare, love and respectGive elders the peace of living among their peersMeet Sulochana At 70, no longer “useful” to her family, Sulochana was taken to Chennai and abandoned at a bus stand. She survived on odd jobs for six years until well-wishers brought her to our NGO partner Akshaya Trust. A medical checkup found a hearing disability, which was treated. Today, she has spent two happy years at Akshaya Trust, where she’s known for her kind heart and warm friendships with other residents.No elder should spend their final years alone. Donate today and give an abandoned senior safety, care and hope.

campaigns.title: Every Child Deserves a Seat: Help Us Raise 150 Desks for children at AVP School
campaigns.description: When Ayushi first walked into Anant Valley Public (AVP) School in 2021, she was just seven years old. She was supposed to be in Grade 2, but she couldn't yet read even two- or three-letter words.But Ayushi wasn't alone.Her story reflects the reality of thousands of children in Tikri Kalan, where over 13,000 school-going children grow up in families that have migrated in search of better livelihood opportunities. Their parents send them to school with the hope of a better future. Yet, even after 14+ years of schooling, most children end up trapped in an inter-generational cycle of poverty.I started AVP to change this reality. To build a school where children don't just attend classes, but actually learn, discover their potential and develop the confidence to imagine a different future for themselves.Ayushi's journey is one of the many stories being rewritten through this initiative.This year, Ayushi and two of her friends were selected for Avasara Academy in Pune, with 100% scholarships covering their education through Grade 12.What makes this even more special? They were among just 10 girls selected from Delhi, and three of those ten came from AVP! When I think about the seven-year-old Ayushi who first walked into our school, struggling to read even two-letter words, and the young girl she is today, I am reminded of what becomes possible when a child gets the opportunity, support and learning environment she deserves.At AVP, that means:a seat in a classroom where learning could happen at her pace; a seat where reading was taught through a carefully designed blend of methods; a seat where children learnt by asking questions, exploring ideas and working on real projects;a seat where teachers had the space to notice what each child needed.A seat at AVP became the beginning of a much bigger journey for Ayushi.And that is what a seat can make possible.AVP began on Children's Day in 2021. We started with what we had, including old furniture that we repaired, reused and upcycled to make our first classrooms ready.Those desks and benches have been part of our school for five years. They have held notebooks, lunchboxes, drawings, classroom projects and countless conversations between friends. We are grateful for all the years they have served us. But they have also worn out. Many are no longer safe for children to use.And as the school has grown, we have outgrown our furniture too. Earlier this year, a few friends of AVP stepped forward to help us buy new desks. Their support helped us address an immediate shortage and reminded us how much a timely contribution can do.Now, we need to take the next step.We are raising ₹7,50,000 to purchase 150 new benches for 300 children. We want every child to have a safe, comfortable place to sit, learn, make things, share ideas and grow. Help us give every child a seat! What can your contribution help us provide?₹100,000 can help us provide benches for a classroom.₹5,000 can help us provide one new bench for 2 children. ₹2,500 can help us provide 2 chairs.Every penny counts!Every contribution brings us closer to a classroom where every child has a safe and comfortable seat.

campaigns.title: Help Disabled Children with Shelter & Care
campaigns.description: Over 20% of the world’s blind people live in India.India has an estimated 4.95 million blind people and 70 million people with vision impairment, including around 2.4 lakh blind children. Disability and poverty often go hand in hand, and for visually impaired children the struggle is even harder. Many face cruel stigma in their own homes and are pushed into isolation.What disabled children faceStigma and misconceptions: Many disabled children are abandoned at birth or face a lifelong struggle. Blindness is often seen as a tragedy, and many believe the disabled can’t study, work or care for themselves. With the right training and tools, they can do nearly everything sighted people can.A struggle for the basics: “How will a disabled person work?” This question keeps talented people out of jobs. Even educated candidates face silent rejection, not because they can’t perform, but because employers won’t include them.How our NGO partners help Our NGO partners give blind and disabled children and young adults shelter, care and education, equipping those overlooked by their families and society with the skills to build a better life.Your donation will help:Fund the rescue of blind and disabled children abandoned by their ownProvide shelter, food, healthcare and educationEquip blind children and young adults with skills for a bright futureMeet Rani Rani, from a small village in Bihar’s Champaran district, lost her eyesight at just four. Years of discrimination followed, but she never gave up on her dream of an education. Seeing her determination, the National Association for the Blind, Delhi supported her higher studies. Today Rani is pursuing her graduation at Miranda House, Delhi, balancing academics and co-curriculars. “If you have the will, you can achieve anything,” she says.Donate today and help a blind or disabled child build the future they deserve.

campaigns.title: Feed the Hungry and Restore Hope
campaigns.description: India ranked 105th of 127 countries in the Global Hunger Index 2024.The Government of India is actively working to fight hunger, and has questioned external reports like the GHI. But for many vulnerable people, empty stomachs remain a daily reality that can’t be overlooked. Whether it’s a school-going child, a child in a slum or a destitute elder, everyone deserves a meal.What hunger feels likeFor the elderly and destitute: Already weak and in pain, many endure abandonment and hunger together. Hunger takes away their dignity and any hope of a decent life.For children in slums and schools: An empty stomach makes it hard to learn and focus, stunting growth and futures. Children suffer the quiet humiliation of falling behind their peers.How our NGO partners help Our NGO partners work on the front lines to deliver more than meals. They bring dignity in a time of need, hope in a moment of despair, and strength for a better tomorrow.Your donation will help:Provide daily nutritious meals to vulnerable communitiesKeep children in school with full stomachs and focused mindsBring dignity and care to forgotten eldersMeet Anand Anand’s parents work hard, but putting food on the table is a daily struggle. He used to sit through class distracted by hunger. Then our NGO partner Prasanna Trust, supported by donors like you, launched a daily breakfast programme. Today, Anand and thousands of children like him start their day nourished, confident and ready to learn.Hunger doesn’t discriminate, and neither should our compassion. Donate today so no child, elder or family goes to bed hungry.

campaigns.title: Support Women and Children to access Good Healthcare!
campaigns.description: Every child deserves a healthy start in life. And every woman deserves access to quality healthcare. In India nearly 35,000 women die every year due to pregnancy and child-birth related complications. 57% Women of reproductive age (15-49 years) are estimated to be anaemic.33% of the disease burden among adults (young parents or to be parents) in India is attributed to unhealthy habits during adolescenceGlobally 1 in 3 women and girls are affected by violence and 32% of ever-married women in India have reported partner violence. Rapid urbanisation and overburdened infrastructure creates low accessibility and affects quality of health and nutrition services in urban informal settlements. Most of the above issues are preventable and are mainly due to the lack of awareness of healthy practices and poor access to quality healthcare services.Source: National Health Family Survey-5, World Health Organization 2017It is said that the health of the child and family begins with a woman. If the woman adopts healthy practices the family will also remain healthy. SNEHA’s intervention primarily focuses on women and to bring in behavior change leading to a lasting impact. While doing so we understand there are various factors impacting the health of women and children and hence we have designed a holistic intervention that focuses on the following:Identifying pregnant women at an early stage and supporting them in accessing antenatal, perinatal and postnatal services from healthcare providers to ensure that they deliver safe and healthy babies.Working with children in the age group of 0-6 years to improve infant and child feeding practices, uptake of immunisation and illness management.Counseling caregivers and decision-makers in the family on the importance of balanced diet, dietary diversity and healthy practices to ensure good health of the woman and child.In the communities we work in generally, the husband/father is the decision maker in the family. We work towards making men an active support system for improved health of the women and children in their family and the community.Supporting the healthcare providers i.e. the health posts and public hospitals by helping strengthen their services and bridging the gap between them and the community, to improve the delivery of services.    We provide counseling services to women undergoing violence or depression and also support them with medical or legal help as required by them.SNEHA is a step towards bridging the health equity gap amongst people living in urban poverty, with a special focus on women and children. Significant Progress so far:48608 Pregnant women with potential complications assisted through referral networks (2016-22)8160 Youth reached through life-skills and health education programmes (2016-22)24420 Survivors of violence counselled for psycho-social support and advanced mental health counselling (2016-22)4765 Mumbai Police personnel trained to respond to survivors of violence (2016-22)86% survivors of violence accessing counselling services reported a reduction in violence and distress levels (2021-22)99% of antenatal care clinics functional in project areas The following story of Saba reflects the challenges faced by women and families in the communities where we work, as our on-ground staff provides information and counseling to change behaviours and attitudes to improve the health of vulnerable women and children. Changing minds through careSaba was three months pregnant when SNEHA’s field staff member met her during the door-to-door visit. Already under treatment for white discharge and irregular menstruation related issues at a nearby hospital, Saba was also found to be mildly anaemic at 10.5 g/dl.We faced stiff resistance from Saba’s husband, because of which we were unable to reach her as Saba delivered in the seventh month of pregnancy. The baby was kept in a glass incubator and when discharged from the hospital after 10 days, he weighed 1.3 kg.During the home visits following the delivery, our field staff member educated Saba about food, health and nutrition practices such as kangaroo mother care, exclusive breastfeeding and maintaining hygiene to ensure better health for the mother and child.We continued with anthropometry of the baby which indicated improvement in height (57.3 cm) and weight (4.36 kg) measurements. When her husband saw his child’s progress, he was convinced of the benefits of SNEHA’s interventions.Our continued efforts have shown positive results with the child now shifted to the normal category and the family continues to follow healthy practices to ensure the well-being of the mother and child.
